title: Teaching Syllabus
excerpt: To study Buddhism is to practice, and to practice exactly as the Buddha taught.

inline.s: To study Buddhism is to practice, and to practice exactly as the Buddha taught.
In its cultivation there is a step by which to enter;
in its realization there is a truth one obtains for oneself.
Diligent and enduring, with a correct method, pressing on without faltering.

The training objectives of the Chan School: to understand the supreme meaning, to bring ten thousand thoughts into one, to return the one to nothingness, to transcend words and thought, and to hold concentration and wisdom in equal practice; to grasp firmly the basic theories of the Dharma and to be able to read the original texts of the scriptures and treatises directly, thereby laying a solid foundation for spreading the Dharma and benefiting living beings.
[Supreme Meaning] The supreme, unsurpassed principle, namely the true mark of all dharmas. The Buddha says:
"All dharmas are false; where they cease, that is called the real, called the true mark, called the Dharma-realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the supreme truth, called the supreme emptiness."
(The Mahaparinirvana Sutra)
The Buddha-Treasury Sutra says:
"The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is wholly without thought and without conception."
It also says:
"Uprooting the root of all conceptual elaboration, forever apart from all, cool and without smoke."
The Essentials of Mind Transmission says:
"When thoughts rest and deliberation is forgotten, the Buddha appears of himself."
Our school's ethos: believe in cause and effect, be able to endure hardship, and never deceive yourself.
[Believing in Cause and Effect]
Master Yinguang says:

"Cause and effect is the great expedient by which the sages govern the world and the Buddhas deliver living beings. Spoken in terms of the Dharma, from the ground of ordinary beings up to the fruit of Buddhahood, no dharma falls outside cause and effect."

(From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Preface to the Record of Curing Both the Root and the Branch to Save the World and Men's Hearts.) Plant melons and you get melons, plant beans and you get beans; as the cause, so the fruit. People commit evil because they do not believe in cause and effect. If a student of Buddhism does not deeply believe in cause and effect and carry it out in daily practice, everything becomes idle talk. Elder Master Xuyun says:

"No matter who you are, and especially if you want to apply effort to practicing the Way, you must first deeply believe in cause and effect. If you do not believe in cause and effect and act recklessly, then never mind that your practice of the Way will not succeed: the three evil paths will not be short of you."

(From the Chan Hall Instruction.) [The three evil paths] Also called the three destinies: the destiny of blood, the destiny of knives, and the destiny of fire. The destiny of blood is the animal realm, for animals are constantly in places where they are killed or devour one another; the destiny of knives is the realm of hungry ghosts, for hungry ghosts are constantly in places of hunger or of the pressing of swords, blades, and staves; the destiny of fire is the hell realm, for hells are constantly in places of freezing ice or of the scorching of fierce fire. These three destinies are another name for the three evil paths.
[Enduring Hardship]
To be able to hold out through dry, dull, and arduous training of great intensity.
"The sword's keen edge is ground and ground; the plum's sweet fragrance from bitter cold is found."
Life needs tempering: ceaselessly challenging oneself and surpassing oneself.
[Never Deceiving Yourself]
Do not deceive yourself. Master Hanshan says:
"Since you have roused faith, you should practice in real earnest
(that is, you should actually practice as the Buddha taught)
, and never deceive yourself."
(From the Collection of Dream-Wandering, Instruction to the Daoists of Yihua.) It is said:
"To catch sparrows with the eyes covered is to deceive oneself."

Even a small creature cannot be taken by deceit and self-satisfaction, let alone the great matter of birth-and-death! [Catching sparrows with the eyes covered] Catching sparrows with the eyes blindfolded. A metaphor for deceiving oneself. [Even a small creature cannot be taken by deceit and self-satisfaction, let alone the great matter of birth-and-death] If even the small matter of catching sparrows can never be accomplished through self-deceit, how much less could the great matter of ending birth-and-death be accomplished through self-deceit?

The purpose of studying Buddhism is to seek the Buddha-way above and to transform living beings below. This too is the great mission of every student of Buddhism. How, then, is this purpose to be attained and this mission fulfilled?

In studying Buddhism one must first rouse the bodhi mind, for rousing the bodhi mind is the solemn vow of the great mission of attaining Buddhahood and delivering living beings; it is the lighthouse for crossing the sea of birth-and-death, and the driving force that rides the wind and breaks the waves.
Master Chewu says:
"If the great mind
(the bodhi mind)

is not roused, then outwardly one cannot resonate with the Buddhas, and inwardly one cannot accord with the inherent nature; above, one cannot perfect the Buddha-way, and below, one cannot widely benefit living beings. How shall the love and affection of beginningless time be freed? How shall the grievances and offenses of beginningless time be dissolved? The karmic offenses of accumulated kalpas are hard to purge by repentance. The roots of goodness of accumulated kalpas are hard to bring to maturity. Whatever one practices, one meets many obstructive conditions. Even if something is accomplished, one finally falls into the partial and small. Therefore one must rouse the great bodhi mind in accord with the inherent nature."
(The Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)
Master Xing'an's Exhortation to Rouse the Bodhi Mind says:

"The essential gate of entering the Way puts rousing the mind first; the urgent task of practice puts establishing the vow before all. Once the vow is established, living beings can be delivered; once the mind is roused, the Buddha-way can be accomplished. If one does not rouse the vast mind and establish a firm vow, then though one pass through dust-like kalpas, one still remains within the round of rebirth; though one may practice, it is all vain toil and hardship. Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'To forget and lose the bodhi mind while cultivating all wholesome dharmas is called the work of Mara.' If forgetting it is already so, how much more never having roused it? Thus we know that one who wishes to study the Tathagata's vehicle must first rouse the bodhisattva vow in full, and must not delay."
Peng Jiqing's Preface to the Posthumous Writings of Master Xing'an says:

"Long ago, when our World-Honored One first accomplished perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed: 'How wondrous! How wondrous! There is no living being who is not endowed with the Tathagata's wisdom. It is only because of deluded thinking, inversion, and attachment that they cannot realize it. If they were free of deluded thinking, then all-wisdom, natural wisdom, and unobstructed wisdom would appear before them.' I could never understand
(I could never understand)
why these living beings cling so bitterly to deluded thinking and attachment and do not let them go, or why, with regard to the Tathagata's wisdom, they shrink
(dan, to flinch at difficulty)
from realizing it. In the end
(zu, finally)

they abandon their father and flee away, drifting for long kalpas, content to be a hired servant and a lowly person, and never think of turning back? There is no other reason: they are simply unawakened. The bodhi mind is another name for awakening. No sooner are they awake than the deluded thinking and attachment before them are wholly the Tathagata's wisdom. For the Tathagata's wisdom has no substance of its own, but takes the deluded thinking of living beings as its substance; and the deluded thinking of living beings has no substance of its own, but takes the Tathagata's wisdom as its substance. It is as when water becomes waves: all the waves are water. From the very beginning they are ultimately to dwell in nirvana without residue. Yet the distinction between awakening and non-awakening must never be concealed from or muddled by oneself. When one is startled into reflection on this
(xu, the sound of flesh parting from bone)

and in a crack of sudden understanding, then the rousing of the bodhi mind comes of itself, swelling forth irresistibly. Once this mind is roused, all-wisdom, natural wisdom, and unobstructed wisdom appear before one; what need is there to seek anything else?"
Elder Master Xuyun says:
"To practice is but this: to know the road's head, whence the way must go; once the road's head is truly known, both birth and death at once are done."
The Surangama Sutra says:
"If the causal ground is not true, the fruit comes crooked and askew."

Therefore it is of the utmost importance that a student of Buddhism possess right knowledge and right view. The curriculum of our school is arranged precisely so that, through systematic study and practice, one establishes right knowledge and right view and carries it out in actual conduct.

Its study is divided into four stages: 1. Ceasing evil and practicing good; 2. Taking precepts as the foundation; 3. Prajna destroying delusion; 4. Concentration and wisdom in equal practice. The specific courses are shown in the table below:

inline.s: Studying Buddhism is a process of turning evil into good, delusion into awakening, and the ordinary into the sage; therefore the study of scriptures and treatises must in the end be carried out in actual practice (in thought and in action).

The method of study and practice is: hearing, then reflection, then cultivation. Hearing means hearing the teachings (including reading the teachings); reflection means reflecting on the meaning of the teachings; cultivation means actually practicing in accord with the meaning of the teachings. Through this process our ignorant views are transformed into right knowledge and right view and carried out in body (action), speech, and mind. In this process permeation is very important: only through constant permeation can one awaken to the Buddha's knowledge and view, give rise to wisdom-understanding, and guide one's own actions.

For beginners, starting directly from the original texts of the scriptures and treatises is quite difficult; it is best to begin with annotated editions. Once one has a certain capacity, one should read the original texts directly, for in this way wisdom-understanding more easily arises. Therefore, when studying with annotated editions, one should consciously cultivate the ability to read the original texts directly. The teaching materials of our school are designed exactly for this: to help the reader understand the scriptures and treatises annotated, and at the same time to cultivate the ability to read the original texts of other scriptures and treatises directly. inline.s: The way of study and practice in our school is: self-study, self-discipline, and self-verification, fulfilling well the four great links of faith, understanding, practice, and realization.

The study and practice of our school is divided into two great parts: the study of scriptures and treatises, and meditation. The teaching materials for the study of scriptures and treatises are the books listed in the curriculum table. Meditation is divided into two gates, contemplating the mind and investigating Chan; the teaching material for contemplating the mind is The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation), and the teaching material for investigating Chan is the book Awareness Chan.

The process of study and practice is: hearing, then reflection, then cultivation. Hearing means hearing the teachings; reflection means reflecting on the meaning of the teachings; cultivation means actually practicing in accord with the meaning of the teachings. This process is meant to transform our ignorant views into right knowledge and right view and to carry them out in body (action), speech, and mind. In this process permeation is very important: only through constant permeation can one awaken to the Buddha's knowledge and view, give rise to wisdom-understanding, and guide one's own actions.
In
the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, precepts are the foundation; one must strictly observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome acts.

[The Three Studies] The study of precepts, the study of concentration, and the study of wisdom. Precepts are the prohibitions, which can prevent people from committing all evil karma of body, speech, and mind; concentration is meditative stillness, which can quiet people's reflections and clarify their minds; wisdom is insight, which can enable people to discover the truth and cut off delusion. By cultivating these three studies one can attain concentration through precepts and give rise to wisdom through concentration, and finally gain the undefiled fruit of the Way; therefore the three studies are also called the "three undefiled studies." [Undefiled] Defilement is another name for affliction, with the meaning of leakage. Afflictions such as greed and anger leak and stream out day and night through the six sense-gates such as eye and ear without cease: this is called defilement. Again, defilement has the meaning of falling away; afflictions can make one fall away into the three evil paths: this is called defilement. Hence dharmas accompanied by affliction are called "with defilement," and dharmas apart from affliction are called "undefiled." [The Five Precepts] Not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, and not drinking alcohol. Not killing means not taking the life of living creatures; not stealing means not taking others' property; not committing sexual misconduct means not performing sexual acts outside marriage; not lying means not speaking deceitful and cheating words; not drinking alcohol means not consuming alcoholic drinks or drugs that numb the human mind. [The Ten Wholesome Acts] Ten kinds of wholesome karma, namely: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not speaking with a divisive tongue, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly, not being greedy, not being angry, and not being deluded. [Divisive tongue] Carrying tales and setting others at odds. [Idle speech] Filthy and defiling speech, meaningless speech, and words with lewd intent.

inline.s: The study and practice of our school is divided into two great parts: the study of scriptures and treatises, and the Chan of awareness. The teaching materials for the study of scriptures and treatises are the books listed in the curriculum table.
When studying a teaching material, first divide it into a number of units, for example by chapter or section.
First, for each unit:
. Skimming. Read the material of this unit three times to build an overall understanding and to know clearly what the specific content of this unit is.
. Close reading. Divide it into paragraphs, write out the gist of each paragraph and the central idea of this unit, and be clear and lucid about difficult characters and difficult sentences.

. Intensive reading. Through intensive reading, the meaning of technical terms must be remembered, one must be able to recite the essential sentences and verses, and one must be able to expound this unit, especially its difficult points and difficult sentences.
Then:
. Mastering the whole book. The requirements are: write out the central idea and the thread of the whole book, and be able to summarize the whole book without looking at the text.

. Permeation. Through constant permeation, awaken to the Buddha's knowledge and view, give rise to wisdom-understanding, and guide one's own actions. This step is very important: one must constantly examine, transform, and elevate oneself amid circumstances and conditions.

The methods of meditation fall into two great gates, contemplating the mind and investigating Chan. Their common path of practice is: ten thousand thoughts converge into one (subduing affliction), the one returns to nothingness, illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature (severing the delusion of view), severing affliction (severing the delusion of thought), attaining the patient acceptance of non-arising, and perfectly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood.

[Illuminating the Mind and Seeing One's Nature] Illuminating the mind means extinguishing mental thoughts; illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature means extinguishing mental thoughts and thoroughly perceiving the inherent nature. [Extinguishing Mental Thoughts] Mental thoughts are of three kinds: coarse thought, fine thought, and subtlest thought. For example, for one who recites the Buddha's name, deluded thoughts are coarse thought, and the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is fine thought. Ordinarily, when both coarse and fine thought have subsided, this is called no-thought, and this is what is generally meant by no-thought. Further, if the subtlest thought also comes to rest, this is ultimate no-thought. Therefore the meaning of the term "no-thought" must be determined according to context. [Subtlest Thought] The subtle arising, ceasing, and flowing of the consciousness-mind is the mark of the alaya-consciousness. When the subtlest thought temporarily rests, the self-nature presents its inherent-nature state: this is illuminating the mind and seeing one's nature. When the subtlest thought rests forever, one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

[Delusion of View] The delusion of view is the confusion and error of ordinary beings with regard to views, such as the five wrong views: the view of self, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions. [Delusion of Thought] The delusion of thought is the confusion and error of ordinary beings with regard to thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt; severing it, one can end birth-and-death and escape the three realms. [Patient Acceptance of Non-Arising] Also called the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas: one understands that all dharmas are from the outset not born, that sentient and insentient alike are condition-born and without nature, and in their very substance are empty; therefore within dharmas without nature the mind rests unmoved in acceptance, personally realizing non-arising.

For details of contemplating the mind, see the teaching material The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation); for details of investigating Chan, see the teaching material Awareness Chan.

2. Close reading. Divide it into paragraphs, write out the gist of each paragraph and the central idea of this chapter, and be clear and lucid about difficult characters and difficult sentences.
3. Intensive reading. Through intensive reading, be able to recite the essential sentences, and be able to expound this chapter, especially its difficult sentences and key points.

4. Actual practice. Focused, continuous, and lasting awareness is the common foundation of contemplating the mind and investigating Chan. The schedule is therefore as follows: in the first academic year, be aware of movements and be aware of sensations; in the second academic year, be aware of the breath; in the third and fourth academic years, be aware of the mind's thoughts; in the fifth and sixth academic years, contemplate the mind or investigate Chan. Awareness of movements, awareness of sensations, awareness of the breath, and awareness of the mind's thoughts are described in detail in the preliminary section of Awareness Chan. For details of contemplating the mind, see the teaching material The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation); for details of investigating Chan, see the teaching material Awareness Chan. As for the specific methods of study and practice and the points requiring attention, these are explained in detail in The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation) and Awareness Chan, and their guiding principle is: start from the difficult, start from the strict, start from actual combat.

blocks.text: 4. The Secret of Success in Study and Practice

inline.s: The secret of success in study and practice: a strong aspiration (as if putting out a fire on one's head), a correct method, and diligent study, hard training, focus, and realization. Start from the difficult and the strict, start from actual combat, and train with a great volume of practice. Practice and apply again and again, press on in the face of difficulty, and amid challenges constantly strengthen your confidence and courage and temper your mental resilience. When tired, when sleepy, when in difficulty, encourage yourself; when temptation comes, when anger rises, when things are dry, dull, and tasteless, admonish yourself: without resolve and willpower, a person accomplishes nothing!

The appearance of difficulty is precisely the turning point of progress. Face difficulty squarely, find the way to solve it, and strive to carry it out, and there will be a new breakthrough. So long as the method is appropriate, together with diligent study and hard training, anyone can achieve outstanding success in study and practice. This is the golden broad road that the patriarchs and great masters have pointed out to us over a thousand years by their own example.

In general, since the way of study and practice is self-study and self-cultivation, you are your own coach, and therefore self-discipline and self-verification are especially important. You must be strict with yourself, control your progress and the results of your practice well, and by all means avoid alternating one day of effort with ten days of neglect, and avoid cooking rice that is half raw. It is very helpful to recall often how you studied when you were at school: how the courses were arranged, how the teachers explained, and how you reviewed, how you completed your assignments, and how you passed the examinations.

The living beings of the Saha world have the sharpest faculty of the ear. Listening while reading is often easier to understand and remember than reading alone. Therefore, when no video of the teaching materials is yet available, one may use a voice-reading tool to read the teaching materials aloud and listen while reading. What is more, one can also permeate one's practice by listening repeatedly.

A voice-reading tool is a tool that helps us learn. Like other tools, the more often it is used, the more proficient one becomes, the more marked the results, and the better one can apply it to the point. If you are not very familiar with installing and adjusting software, ask a friend who is familiar with it to help, and you need only use it. (For the installation and settings of voice-reading tools, see in this Study Garden the article

The first stage of the curriculum is "ceasing evil and cultivating virtue," the second stage is "taking precepts and concentration as the foundation," the third stage is "prajna destroying delusion," and the fourth stage is "concentration and wisdom in equal practice."

inline.s: The courses of study at this stage are: the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, Liao Fan's Four Lessons, the Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Encounter with the Kitchen God, and the Treatise on Response and Retribution. The core of the study is: "Support and serve your parents, serve and attend upon your teachers, cherish compassion and do not kill, and cultivate the ten wholesome acts."

The teaching materials are: Lecture Record on the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, Annotated Liao Fan's Four Lessons, Annotated Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Encounter with the Kitchen God, and Annotated Treatise on Response and Retribution.

Actual practice: 1. Hearing, reflection, and cultivation; 2. Recite one copy of the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva every day; 3. Recite the holy name of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva ten thousand times; 4. Be aware of movements (for details, see the book Awareness Chan).
Introduction to the teaching materials:

rows.s: Lecture Record on the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

With the peerless power of his vow, "Only when all living beings are delivered will I realize bodhi; only when the hells are empty will I attain Buddhahood," Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva delivers us suffering living beings. Reciting the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva not only averts calamity and hardship, dissolves enmity and unties knots, and makes all one does auspicious, but also brings many, many inconceivable merits and benefits.
This book explains the Sutra of the Original Vows of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva in detail and is a very good guide for study and practice.
Annotated Liao Fan's Four Lessons

Liao Fan's Four Lessons is a precious book for remaking one's destiny; for four hundred years countless people of lofty purpose have taken it as their standard, and thereby completely changed their own destinies.

This book provides detailed annotation, helping on the one hand to understand the meaning of the original text, and on the other hand helping students to improve their ability to read classical Chinese, thus laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Annotated Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Encounter with the Kitchen God

The Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi's Encounter with the Kitchen God is a companion piece to Liao Fan's Four Lessons, and is likewise a precious book for remaking one's destiny; for four hundred years countless people of lofty purpose have taken it as their standard, and thereby completely changed their own destinies.

This book provides detailed annotation, helping on the one hand to understand the meaning of the original text, and on the other hand helping students to improve their ability to read classical Chinese, thus laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Records of Wang Fengyi's Excellent Words

The Records of Wang Fengyi's Excellent Words are the recorded sayings of the venerable good man Wang Fengyi (1864-1937). He was a hired farmhand in the countryside who had never attended school, yet because he earnestly practiced loyalty and filial piety, he became enlightened through sincerity. At the age of thirty-five, on his way to rescue his friend Yang Bo, a strange sign appeared in the heavens midway, and in the black night he saw bright day, whereupon he understood the Way. At thirty-eight his father passed away, and after keeping vigil at the grave for a hundred days he attained great awakening; he then devised the method of healing illness through the principle of the nature, explaining illness to transform the world and universally delivering the multitude. When the good man Wang spoke of the Way, his words seemed homely and plain, yet their meaning was profound, all flowing forth from the inherent nature; unbound by scriptures and teachings, he taught with expedient means, lively and natural, and his essential aim was to teach people to fulfill the way of loyalty and filial piety, transform their nature, and establish their destiny. Wang Fengyi tells us: wealth and honor or poverty and lowliness, good fortune or misfortune, suffering or joy in life are all held in one's own hands.
Annotated Treatise on Response and Retribution

Master Yinguang says: "The Treatise of the Most High on Response and Retribution gathers the supreme principles that blessing follows the good and calamity the perverse, that virtue brings reward and license brings ruin, and gives them forth in arguments that shake heaven and earth and startle the eye and heart. What is good? What is evil? What good reward does the doer of good receive? What evil reward does the doer of evil receive? It penetrates the root and source, clear as looking at a person. Moreover, the reason foolish people refuse to do good and do evil at will is that a selfish, self-seeking heart drives them to it. Now they know that the selfish and self-seeking instead lose great benefit and gain great calamity; would they dare not strive to do good, hoping that calamity may be extinguished and blessing gathered? From this we may say that this book benefits people deeply! Hence many great Confucian scholars of old cultivated themselves in secret according to it. ... To speak of this book in the ultimate, it stops at becoming an immortal; but if one practices it with the great bodhi mind, one can transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, end birth-and-death, sever the three delusions and realize the dharmakaya, perfect blessing and wisdom and accomplish the Buddha-way; how much more so than the mere human and heavenly small fruit of becoming an immortal!" (Preface to the Direct Explanation of the Treatise of the Most High on Response and Retribution)

blocks.text: Stage Two: Taking Precepts as the Foundation

inline.s: The texts studied in this stage are the Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters, the Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings, the Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths, the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and the Great Mindfulness Sutra. The core of this stage's study is: "Take refuge in the Three Jewels, observe all the precepts in full, and never violate the rules of dignity."

The companion commentaries are: Annotated Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters, Annotated Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings, Annotated Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths, Annotated Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and Annotated Great Mindfulness Sutra.

Practice: First, hear, reflect, and cultivate. Second, take turns reciting the Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters, the Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings, the Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths, the Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching, and the Great Mindfulness Sutra, one each day. Third, be aware of the breath and aware of the sensations (see the book Awareness Chan for details).

rows.s: Annotated Sutra of the Forty-Two Chapters

This sutra is the first Buddhist scripture to be transmitted to our land. Its content is at once shallow and deep, gradual and sudden, partial and perfect, provisional and real, and includes both the Lesser and the Greater Vehicles. It is a scripture of outline and principle. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.
Annotated Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings

The Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings sets out to clarify the eight realizations of the bodhisattva (the "great beings" of the sutra): the realization of impermanence and no-self, the realization of few desires and non-doing, the realization of contented poverty and guarding the Way, the realization of constant diligence, the realization of wide learning and growth in wisdom, the realization of even-mindedness toward enemies and kin, the realization of the harm of the five desires, and the realization of the great mind of universal deliverance, so as to awaken oneself and awaken others. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.
Annotated Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths

In the Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths the Buddha says that all dharmas are never apart from the mind, and that one should cultivate the ten wholesome acts and sever all suffering. This is the most fundamental practice of the Buddha's teaching. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.
Annotated Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching

The Sutra of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching is the final instruction the Buddha gave to his disciples before entering nirvana. There he singles out the essence and reiterates, in earnest, how to cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom so as to escape affliction and birth-and-death. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.
Annotated Great Mindfulness Sutra

In the study of Buddhism what matters most is actual practice and real realization, putting an end to birth-and-death and escaping the round of rebirth. Hence the first task is to subdue affliction and then to sever it. For a student of the Pure Land school, as long as one can subdue affliction, one can single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name and be reborn in the Western Pure Land. In the Great Mindfulness Sutra the Buddha gives a full and detailed teaching on how to subdue affliction and sever it: to maintain an unbroken, continuous awareness and contemplation of the arising and ceasing and changing of body, mind, and world. This is the simplest and most direct method of going from the knowledge of suffering to the ending of suffering. This commentary helps the reader grasp the meaning within the text.

inline.s: The texts studied in this stage are the Diamond Sutra, the Heart Sutra, the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and the Direct Explanation of the True Mind. The core of this stage's study is: "Rouse the bodhi mind, deeply believe in cause and effect, recite the Mahayana scriptures, and encourage fellow cultivators."

The companion commentaries are: Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra, Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra, Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and Detailed Explanation of the Direct Explanation of the True Mind.

Practice: First, hear, reflect, and cultivate. Second, recite the Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra once each every day. Third, be aware of the mind's thoughts (see the book Awareness Chan for details).

rows.s: Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra

For a thousand years, why has the Diamond Sutra been known in every household, expounded in countless lectures, and annotated countless times? The reason lies not only in the immeasurable merit and virtue gained by receiving, upholding, and reciting it, but also because people have come to realize that the Diamond Sutra reveals a truth of boundless yet most mysterious power, a wish-fulfilling king of jewels for leaving suffering, escaping death, and attaining Buddhahood. Therefore they pursue and contemplate it tirelessly: What is the Diamond Sutra speaking of? What, indeed, is it speaking of? To answer these questions, this explanation was composed.

The commentary in this book is thorough and lucid. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra

The Heart Sutra is on everyone's lips, for it is the great dharma that destroys illusion and carries all beings beyond all suffering and calamity. When Master Xuanzang journeyed west in search of the scriptures, he crossed alone an eight-hundred-li desert of yellow sand, where no bird flew above and no beast walked below, and he often encountered all manner of ghosts and demons of monstrous shapes thronging before and behind him; yet the master "thought only of the Heart Sutra, and at the sound of it they vanished at once." This shows that the Heart Sutra is not only exquisite in meaning, but also that receiving, upholding, and reciting it takes effect most marvelously. However, the meaning of this sutra is profound and hard to grasp; if the meaning is not reached, the contemplative view is unclear; and if the contemplative view is unclear, one wanders in confusion with no direction. For this reason this explanation was composed.

The commentary in this book is thorough and lucid. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch is the only work of Chinese Buddhism honored with the title "sutra." It sets forth systematically and comprehensively the theory and practice of the sudden teaching of "seeing one's nature and realizing Buddhahood," and its appearance marks the formal establishment of the Chan school in China, blazing with a ten-thousand-rayed light. The Platform Sutra is the great practice of the Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra. The Diamond Sutra and the Heart Sutra speak of the true reality of all dharmas, while the Platform Sutra, drawing on them, uses concrete practice to realize that true reality, accomplish the patience with the unborn, and so reach the perfect clarity that forever leaves all marks and directly attains Buddhahood.

This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Selected Annotations on the Buddha-Store Sutra

In the study of the Buddha-dharma, the first requirement is proper view. What is proper view? To take the scriptures as one's basis, the Buddha's mind as one's own mind, the Buddha's words as one's own words, and the Buddha's conduct as one's own conduct. That is proper view. To this end, the "Chapter on the True Reality of All Dharmas, First," the "Chapter on Buddha-Recollection, Second," the "Chapter on Pure Dharma, Sixth," the "Chapter on the Ancient Past, Seventh," and the "Chapter on the Ascertainment of Precepts, Ninth" have been chosen from the Buddha-Store Sutra and annotated.
Detailed Explanation of the Direct Explanation of the True Mind

The Direct Explanation of the True Mind treats the true mind (the inherent nature) comprehensively under the following fifteen aspects: the right faith of the true mind, the other names of the true mind, the wondrous substance of the true mind, the wondrous functioning of the true mind, the unity and difference of substance and function, the true mind in delusion, the true mind stilling delusion, the four postures of the true mind, where the true mind dwells, the true mind's escape from death, the primary and auxiliary practices, the virtue of the true mind, the verification of the true mind's merit, the true mind's non-knowing, and where the true mind goes. It clarifies the true mind (the inherent nature) that everyone inherently possesses, the root of delusion and awakening, and the path of practice and the state attained.

blocks.text: Stage Four: Concentration and Wisdom in Equal Practice

inline.s: The texts studied in this stage are: Detailed Explanation of the Treatise on the Two Entries and Four Practices, Detailed Explanation of the Essentials of Mind Cultivation, Essentials of Chan and Pure Land, and The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation).
Practice: First, read and apply hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Second, meditate (see the book Awareness Chan for details).
[Equal practice of concentration and wisdom] The Treatise on Severing Contemplation says:
"When the mind-nature is still and extinct, this is concentration; always realizing this still extinction is wisdom."

This means: when the mind-nature dwells in a state of still extinction, it is called concentration; knowing clearly at all times that the mind-nature is in this still extinction is called wisdom. Therefore concentration is stillness, and wisdom is illumination. To hold concentration and wisdom in equal practice is to be still yet illuminating, illuminating yet still. Master Dayu says:
"In stillness and illumination, in illumination and stillness, beware above all of forcing; to become a Buddha or a patriarch there is no other secret."
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment the Buddha says:
"All Tathagatas, in their originating ground, rely upon the perfect illumination of the pure, clear awareness-image and forever sever ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way."

Here, the pure, clear awareness-image is concentration, and perfect illumination is wisdom; the perfect illumination of the pure, clear awareness-image is precisely the equal practice of concentration and wisdom.

[Stillness-illumination] Still yet illuminating: when a single thought does not arise (stillness), to be aware that this single thought does not arise (illumination) is like a pearl emitting light that still shines back upon the pearl's own body. Stillness is the substance, illumination the substance's functioning. Concentration is the substance, wisdom the substance's functioning. [Originating ground] This refers to the time when the Buddha was on the causal ground. [Causal ground] From the stage of an ordinary being first rousing the mind to study Buddhism up to the perfect realization of Buddhahood, the whole process is called the "causal ground."

rows.s: Detailed Explanation of the Treatise on the Two Entries and Four Practices

The Treatise on the Two Entries and Four Practices is the essential teaching on entering the Way that Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted personally. The words are few but the meaning is rich, embracing both principle and practice; truly it is the outline of the school and the guide of the practitioner. This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Detailed Explanation of the Essentials of Mind Cultivation

The Essentials of Mind Cultivation explains the essential method of mind cultivation from three aspects: seeing one's nature and realizing Buddhahood, sudden awakening with gradual cultivation, and the equal practice of concentration and wisdom. First, the aim of seeing one's nature lies in realizing that one's own mind is the true Buddha and one's own nature is the true Dharma. Second, to see through that the ordinary being is the Buddha is sudden awakening; to be transformed by the power of the Dharma is gradual cultivation. The tracks of the thousand sages are no more than these two gates. Third, empty stillness and numinous knowing are the substance (concentration) and functioning (wisdom) of the inherent nature; therefore one should be ever still and ever knowing, with substance and functioning never apart, holding concentration and wisdom in equal practice.

This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation)

The distinguishing feature of The Essential Mind of White Cloud (The Precious Book of Mind Contemplation) is that it is keen, swift, sudden, and perfect. How great the good fortune of those who read it and practice it! One should advance with understanding and practice together, understanding in the very act of practice, and practice in the very act of understanding. Do the work of taming the mind day by day: when the thoughts become clear, wisdom is born; never apart from the inherent nature is the field of merit. When one contemplates until a single thought does not arise, one is in accord with prajna. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "All Tathagatas, in their originating ground, rely upon the perfect illumination of the pure, clear awareness-image and forever sever ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way."

This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Essentials of Chan and Pure Land

Master Hanshan says: "In the age of the Dharma's end there are many who practice, yet few who gain the real benefit; many who toil with great effort, yet few who gain real power. Why is this? It is because they do not light upon a direct point at which to begin."

The Essentials of Chan and Pure Land is compiled from Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream-Wandering, and it focuses on how to practice in earnest. In its several chapters Master Hanshan gives incisive teachings on the essentials and the points of entry of both the Chan and the Pure Land schools. As students savor them repeatedly and advance in understanding and practice together, they will surely gain the real benefit.

This book provides a detailed commentary. On the one hand it helps the reader grasp the meaning of the original text, and on the other it helps students improve their ability to read classical prose, laying a foundation for reading the scriptures and treatises directly.
Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment has twelve chapters, in which the Buddha, through dialogue with twelve great bodhisattvas, proclaims the wondrous principle of the Tathagata's perfect enlightenment (the perfect awakening of the inherent nature) and the method of practice.

Master Hanshan says: "As for what is most simple yet most refined, most immediate yet most essential, nothing surpasses the supreme Dharma-gate of perfect enlightenment. Its text is no more than thirteen thousand words, yet it unites the boundless ocean of teachings and encompasses the whole Dharma-realm; it rounds to the single source of the mind and passes through the purport of the three contemplations. Partial and proper interchanged, single and repeated cultivated in fullness, it exhausts the lord of delusion, strips away the maladies of Chan, and the wondrous gate of awakening the mind surmounts directly in a single leap. This is what is called the true sutra of the Dharma-realm, the wondrous practice of becoming a Buddha. Sudden awakening and sudden realization are like viewing a fruit in one's palm. The purport of the coming from the West, the secret and wondrous meaning, holds nothing beyond this. All who study Buddhism take it as their guide." (From the Postscript to the Engraved Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment)
Awareness Chan

This is the practice textbook of the Chan School, whose aim is: ten thousand thoughts converge into one, and the one returns to nothingness, thereby seeing one's nature and realizing Buddhahood. As for how to investigate Chan, this book gives a systematic explanation and concrete steps of practice, truly as the ancients said: "In its cultivation there is a step by which to enter; in its realization there is a truth one obtains for oneself."

blocks.text: 6. Practicing Chan and Pure Land Together

inline.s: A Chan practitioner came to visit and asked: "At the moment of death, if one has not yet seen one's nature (fully perceived the inherent nature), or has seen one's nature but not yet severed the delusion of thought, what plan can put an end to birth-and-death?"

[Delusion of view and delusion of thought] The delusion of view and the delusion of thought. The delusion of view is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in matters of view, such as the five false views of self-view, extremist view, perverted view, view-attachment, and precept-attachment; the delusion of thought is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in matters of thought, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, arrogance, and doubt. These two delusions are the root by which sentient beings drift through the three realms and endure birth-and-death in vain; severing them enables one to end birth-and-death and escape the three realms.
Answer: Practice Chan and Pure Land together.
Question: Why practice Chan and Pure Land together?

Answer: Mazu established the monastery (the Chan temple), and Baizhang laid down the pure rules (the "essential rules of the monastery"). These pure rules were established for the Chan practitioners in the monastery, and they say at the outset:
"A monastery flourishes by having no affairs; in practice, Buddha-recitation is the most certain."

The second sentence, "in practice, Buddha-recitation is the most certain," means that for the sake of certainty, a Chan practitioner, while investigating Chan, should also believe, vow, and recite the Buddha's name, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land (practicing Chan and Pure Land together). This is because, by reciting the Buddha's name and being reborn in the Western Pure Land, one ends birth-and-death merely by subduing affliction; whereas one who investigates Chan, in order to end birth-and-death, must sever the delusions of view and thought. In comparison the former is far easier, and so is the more certain path. Many patriarchs and great masters practiced Chan and Pure Land together, making the Pure Land their final return. For example, Master Yongming Yanshou, Master Hanshan, Master Chewu, and others. National Master Puzhao, the author of the Essentials of Mind Cultivation, also practiced the two together and wrote the Essential Gate of Buddha-Recitation. Master Yongming Yanshou composed the Four Selections, advocating the joint practice of Chan and the Pure Land. His verse reads:
With Chan but without the Pure Land, nine of ten men miss the way; when the shadow of the karmic state appears, in a flash he goes along with it.
Without Chan but with the Pure Land, of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go; once one beholds Amitabha, how can one worry not to awaken?
With Chan and with the Pure Land, he is like a tiger wearing horns: a teacher of men in this life, in the next a Buddha and a patriarch.
Without Chan and without the Pure Land, the iron bed and the bronze pillar await; through myriad kalpas and a thousand births, there is no one to rely upon.

[Selection] Distinguishing and choosing among meanings. [The Four Selections] Four judgments of selection. [With Chan] Seeing one's nature (fully perceiving the inherent nature). [With the Pure Land] True faith and earnest vow, reciting the Buddha's name with single-minded focus. [Without Chan] Not having seen one's nature. [Without the Pure Land] Not having accomplished "true faith and earnest vow, reciting the Buddha's name with single-minded focus."
Question: As long as one has faith and vow and holds the name, it is "having the Pure Land." Why require that one's Buddha-recitation reach single-minded focus?

Answer: Master Ouyi (the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school), in his Essentials of the Amitabha Sutra, expressly teaches: without the wondrous practice of single-minded Buddha-recitation, one cannot prove his true faith or fulfill his earnest vow. (The original says:
"Practice is to hold fast the name, with single-minded focus." "Without the wondrous practice of upholding the Name, one cannot fulfill one's vow and prove one's faith."
Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) says:
"Single-minded focus is the final destination of the pure karma and the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, then it is never certain."

(From the Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu.) If one's Buddha-recitation has not yet reached single-minded focus, how can it be called "having the Pure Land," and "of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go"?
Now I shall explain the Four Selections as follows:
[With Chan but without the Pure Land, nine of ten men miss the way; when the shadow of the karmic state appears, in a flash he goes along with it.]

If one investigates Chan and sees one's nature but has not severed the delusions of view and thought (this is true of nine out of ten among those who have awakened), then when the shadow of the karmic state appears at death, he immediately follows the karmic force to be reborn, quite unable to be his own master. Yet because the awakening has already severed the delusion of view, he will not be born again in an evil realm.

[Nine of ten men miss the way] Among those who have seen their nature, at least nine-tenths have not severed the delusions of view and thought. For them, to practice Chan alone is a mistaken path, because they cannot leave the round of rebirth. [Miss chuo] Error, mistake. [Shadow of the karmic state] The state of the intermediate body, that is, the manifestation at the moment of death of the karmic forces of good and evil from this life and all past lives. The instant this state appears, in the blink of an eye one goes to be reborn in a good or evil realm following the most violent of those karmic forces, without the slightest mastery over oneself. [In a flash] Suddenly, rapidly.
[Without Chan but with the Pure Land, of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go; once one beholds Amitabha, how can one worry not to awaken?]

Although one has not yet seen one's nature, with true faith and earnest vow and single-minded Buddha-recitation one can be reborn in the Western Pure Land with absolute certainty (of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go). Having gone to the Western Pure Land and seen Amitabha Buddha, one accomplishes Buddhahood in a single lifetime. How could one still worry about not seeing one's nature?
[With Chan and with the Pure Land, he is like a tiger wearing horns: a teacher of men in this life, in the next a Buddha and a patriarch.]

Having already seen one's nature, and with true faith and earnest vow and single-minded Buddha-recitation, one is a teacher of men in this life. At the moment of death he is reborn in the highest grade in the Western Pure Land, accomplishing Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

Single-minded Buddha-recitation has the single-minded focus of affairs and the single-minded focus of principle. For one who has seen his nature (who has Chan) to recite the Buddha's name is the single-minded focus of principle; having gone to the Western Pure Land he is reborn in the highest grade, and to be a teacher and a Buddha is entirely natural. As for the single-minded focus of affairs and the single-minded focus of principle, see our academy's textbook
Detailed Explanation of the Record of Feeling the Samadhi of Buddha-Recollection
[Without Chan and without the Pure Land, the iron bed and the bronze pillar await; through myriad kalpas and a thousand births, there is no one to rely upon.]

If one has not seen his nature and has not accomplished "true faith and earnest vow, single-minded Buddha-recitation," then if at death he cannot keep his right mindfulness clear, he is drawn by karmic force and reborn among the six realms. Because he has not severed the delusion of view, he will revolve through the evil realms, and the time spent in hell (the iron bed and the bronze pillar) is the longest. The Buddha says: "Those who gain a human body are like the soil on a fingernail; those who lose a human body are like the soil of the great earth."
Question: To practice Chan and at the same time believe, vow, and recite the Buddha's name, is this not mixing things up, standing with one foot in each of two boats?

Answer: It is not standing in two boats, but boarding the one boat by which one can reach the other shore in this very life. The aim of our study of Buddhism is to become a Buddha and to deliver sentient beings. To become a Buddha, one must first put an end to birth-and-death by division and escape the round of rebirth, and then end birth-and-death by transformation and realize the Buddha-fruit. For this one life, the urgent task is to end birth-and-death by division and escape the round of rebirth. Those who can sever the delusions of view and thought lie outside the scope of our discussion. For those who cannot sever these two delusions, there are three boats: cultivating the Pure Land, cultivating Chan, and cultivating Chan and the Pure Land together. Cultivating the Pure Land is the business of students of the Pure Land school; we discuss only the two boats of cultivating Chan and of cultivating the two together.

If one cultivates Chan alone, there are two outcomes: having Chan without the Pure Land, and having neither Chan nor the Pure Land. Neither can end birth-and-death and escape the round of rebirth. In particular, to cultivate Chan yet not see one's nature has extremely grave consequences: the iron bed and the bronze pillar. Therefore, to end birth-and-death and escape the round of rebirth there is only one boat: to practice Chan and the Pure Land together. As for whether this joint practice is a mixing, so long as one uses it well, it is not only unmixed but mutually enhancing; you will soon know this for yourself. Think about it: if it were a mixing, why would Patriarch Yongming say "with Chan and with the Pure Land, he is like a tiger wearing horns: a teacher of men in this life, in the next a Buddha and a patriarch"? Patriarch Yongming himself was a man who had come through the joint practice, and in his own practice he personally proved that the two together enhance each other, "like a tiger wearing horns, a teacher of men in this life, in the next a Buddha and a patriarch."

[Birth-and-death by division] Sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because they are recompensed by good and evil karma, have a fixed limit to their lifespan and a distinct division to their bodies; therefore their birth-and-death is called "birth-and-death by division." One who ends birth-and-death by division is freed of the round of rebirth and has escaped the three realms. [Birth-and-death by transformation] The sages of the three vehicles, having severed the delusions of view and thought and ended birth-and-death by division, in the course of cultivation have deluded thoughts gradually extinguished and realization gradually increased; this shifting of delusion and awakening differs in each period, and the passage from a former period to a later one is, as it were, a dying and a becoming, whose change is subtle, mysterious, and inconceivable. Hence it is called "birth-and-death by transformation." One who ends birth-and-death by transformation fully realizes the Buddha-fruit.
Question: Then why cultivate Chan?
Answer: Cultivating Chan is suited to the following circumstances:
First, those who in this life can sever the delusions of view and thought, or even those who seek to transcend the Dharma-body, should cultivate Chan.
Second, the distinctive character of Chinese Buddhism lies in Chan. Those who wish to thoroughly understand Chinese Buddhism and revive Chinese Buddhism should cultivate Chan.
Third, those who wish to be a horned tiger and widely deliver sentient beings should cultivate Chan.

Fourth, in terms of practice, the Chan school has a vast and profound body of theory, methods, and cases, perfect and sudden, keen and swift. Those whose faculties accord with Chan and who delight in it should cultivate Chan.
Question: How does one practice Chan and Pure Land together?

Answer: Investigating Chan in order to see one's nature has three stages: first, the coarse thought subsides (ten thousand thoughts converge into one); second, the fine thought subsides (the one returns to nothingness); third, the subtlest thought comes to rest and one fully perceives the inherent nature. Having, by investigating Chan, brought ten thousand thoughts to converge into one, or the one to return to nothingness, or even seen one's nature, a practitioner's Buddha-recitation can reach single-minded focus. But to be reborn in the Western Pure Land, besides single-minded Buddha-recitation, one must also have true faith and an earnest vow. Trust means steadfastly trusting in the Buddha's power. When Amitabha Buddha was on the causal ground he made forty-eight vows, each one to deliver sentient beings; and the Buddha's compassionate power gathers in sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If, at the moment of death, I concentrate my right mindfulness within, like a child remembering his mother, I can surely move the Buddha to come and welcome me. Vow means being willing to be reborn in this very lifetime in the Western Pure Land, no longer sinking and rising for many lives and many kalpas in this defiled place, going from delusion into delusion. And having vowed to be reborn in the Western Pure Land, one vows to return to the Saha world to deliver all sentient beings. Therefore, in the joint practice of Chan and the Pure Land, one must solidly and genuinely exert effort in true faith and earnest vow, and attain single-minded Buddha-recitation, so that at death one earnestly seeks rebirth in the Western Pure Land, concentrating right mindfulness within and drawing the Buddha's welcome from without. As for true faith, earnest vow, and the method of Buddha-recitation, see our academy's textbook
Aware Buddha-Recitation

[Coarse thought, fine thought, and subtlest thought] For example, for one who is reciting the Buddha's name, wandering thoughts are the coarse thought, and the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is the fine thought. Usually, when both the coarse and the fine thoughts have subsided, this is called no-thought, which is the no-thought ordinarily meant. Beyond this, if the subtlest thought also comes to rest, this is the ultimate no-thought. [Subtlest thought] The subtle arising, ceasing, and flowing of the cognitive mind is the characteristic mark of the alaya consciousness.
Question: What are the differences and the similarities between Chan and the Pure Land?

Answer: In terms of practice, whichever gate one takes, the path is all the same: ten thousand thoughts converge into one, the one returns to nothingness, one sees one's nature, severs the delusions of view and thought, attains the patience with the unborn, and fully realizes the Buddha-fruit.

The Pure Land school is to recite Amitabha Buddha of the Western Pure Land and to seek rebirth there. As long as through Buddha-recitation one reaches the convergence of ten thousand thoughts into one (single-minded focus), at death one is certainly reborn in the Western Pure Land. When the flower opens and one sees the Buddha, one at once attains the patience with the unborn, and then fully realizes the Buddha-fruit. If, having attained single-minded focus, one wishes to raise the grade of rebirth, one may further cultivate the samadhi of Buddha-recitation so that the one returns to nothingness and one sees one's nature (as for the samadhi of Buddha-recitation, see our academy's textbook
Detailed Explanation of the Record of Feeling the Samadhi of Buddha-Recollection
. Of course, one may also continue further, severing the delusions of view and thought and then attaining the patience with the unborn.

Investigating Chan, by raising the topic of meditation, brings ten thousand thoughts into one, then the one returns to nothingness, then one sees one's nature; afterward one severs the delusions of view and thought; then one attains the patience with the unborn.

Contemplating the mind, by observing the flowing consciousness of the karma presently manifesting in one's own mind, brings ten thousand thoughts into one, then the one returns to nothingness, then one sees one's nature; afterward one severs the delusions of view and thought; then one attains the patience with the unborn.

The Pure Land school, with faith, vow, and the upholding of the Name, needs only to reach the convergence of ten thousand thoughts into one (single-minded focus) in order to end birth-and-death. The two great gates of the Chan school, investigating Chan and contemplating the mind, both require one to sever the delusions of view and thought before one can end birth-and-death.
Question: The fourth patriarch of the Chan school, Master Daoxin, says:

"The objects and conditions of the world are neither good nor bad; good and bad arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, whence can false emotion arise? Since false emotion does not arise, the true mind is free to know all things. Only let the mind be at ease according to itself, with no more opposing treatment; this is called the everlasting Dharma-body, without any change."
This instruction is the most direct method of practice. Why must one "converge ten thousand thoughts into one, return the one to nothingness, see one's nature, and so on"?

Answer: This instruction of the fourth patriarch was given to Master Farong of Mount Niutou (see the Record of the Five Lamps). At that time Farong had already cultivated to the point of "the marvel of a hundred birds bringing flowers," and "the fourth patriarch, observing the atmosphere from afar, knew that there was an extraordinary person on that mountain (Mount Niutou), and so went in person to seek him out." Therefore the fourth patriarch gave him, in a pointed way, the gate of spontaneous operation: "Only let the mind be at ease according to itself, with no more opposing treatment." But for ordinary people, if when confronted with circumstances they cannot manage not to "forcibly name" them, then they should first enter the gate of opposing treatment and begin with the convergence of ten thousand thoughts into one and so forth. In fact, before Farong met the fourth patriarch, he too had begun with the convergence of ten thousand thoughts into one and so forth, or else in a former life he had begun there. This principle is thoroughly set forth in the Essentials of Mind Cultivation;
